The prior word of God, namely the postponement of judgment and punishment until the Last Day, is what prevented the matter from being settled in this world, where the wrongdoers would have been destroyed and the righteous saved. Most agree that the 'single community' means the true religion, but they differ about its period. Mujahid and al-Suddi, reported by Ibn Kathir, place it between Adam and the killing of one of his sons by the other, or up to Noah; al-Dahhak says it refers to the people of the ark; al-Kalbi and Ata' place it in adherence to Abraham's religion until Amr ibn Luhayy changed it. Al-Razi judges it more likely that it means unity in Islam, since the threat is tied to a division arising from disbelief. As for the prior word, al-Tabari, al-Kalbi and Ibn Kathir take it as the postponement of punishment for this community; Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari take it as the deferral of judgment to the Day of Resurrection; al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi take it as the decree fixing lifespans; al-Razi reports other views, including the saying that my mercy precedes my wrath.

Most link the verse to the refutation of idol worship and its alleged intercession. When the polytheists ask for a sign to be sent down, the Prophet is told to answer that the unseen belongs to God alone, and that all must wait. At-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the threat was fulfilled at Badr, according to at-Tabari. Some readings, such as laqada and tushrikun, are noted by Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya without the meaning depending on them.

This verse reports the demand of the Meccan disbelievers that the Prophet ﷺ be given a clear sign from his Lord, such as the she-camel or Moses' staff, so that they might know he was truthful. According to the commentators, they disregarded the great signs already sent to him, above all the Qur'an itself, and treated them as if nothing had been revealed. God instructs His Messenger to answer that the unseen belongs to God alone, who alone knows why the requested sign is not sent, and to tell them to wait, for he is waiting with them.

The commentators agree that the verse refers the question to God's knowledge and wisdom, and they read the command to wait in two ways: waiting for the requested sign, or waiting for God's judgment between the two sides, by which truth will be shown over falsehood. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that this warning was fulfilled at Badr. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that no prophet was ever given a sign that forces faith, and that miracles are presented for reflection so that some are guided and others go astray.

They differ on the meaning of the unseen. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi take it as the reason the sign is withheld or the time of its coming. Al-Razi argues that prophethood does not depend on such a sign and is established whether or not it is sent. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan understand it as what no created being can know.

Ibn Kathir adds that God did not grant these requests because He knew their stubbornness, and he cites verses stating that those against whom God's word has been fulfilled will not believe even if every sign comes to them.

The commentators explain that this verse addresses the people of Mecca: when God grants them mercy after hardship, such as rain after drought, ease after distress or health after illness, they quickly turn to scheming against God's signs, that is, mocking and denying them. Some understand the scheme as denial, others as hypocrisy or as attributing the blessing to the stars. All agree that 'God is swifter in plotting' means that His punishment reaches them faster than their own scheming, and that the recording of their deeds by the angelic scribes shows that their actions are accounted for. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi take the scheming to be mockery and denial, while al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi also report that it may mean disbelief, rejection or hypocrisy, and Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi see it as disparaging the signs and manoeuvring to repel them. Tradition links the verse to a seven-year famine that struck Quraysh after the Prophet ﷺ prayed against them, followed by rain which they received without believing. Ibn 'Ashur dates this famine to the period of Surat al-Dukhan. Readers differ between 'yamkurun' and 'tamkurun', as al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan note. Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur explain that ascribing scheming to God is a figure of speech by correspondence. Al-Razi observes that the verse exposes the stubborn character of these people, so that further miracles would not benefit them.

The verse describes a sea voyage: God makes you travel on land and sea; when you are aboard the ship and a gentle wind carries you, you rejoice, then a violent wind comes and waves strike from every side; you think you are about to perish, so you call on God alone, sincerely, promising to be grateful if He saves you. The commentators agree that this sincerity in distress reveals the natural inclination towards monotheism, and that rescue at sea is a clear sign of God's favour. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the prayer was purely directed to God and did not associate idols; al-Hasan sees it as a faith compelled by necessity, a view al-Razi also reports. The readings differ: most read "yusayyirukum" (He makes you travel), while Ibn Amir and Abu Ja'far read "yunshirukum" (He scatters you). Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take the whole conditional clause as the endpoint of "until", not merely boarding the ship. Commentators see in the passage an argument against the polytheists, who call upon God in peril and then transgress once saved; their wrongdoing falls back on themselves, which Ibn Kathir supports with a hadith on transgression. Ibn 'Ashur stresses the reminder of this blessing and the call to gratitude. Al-Alusi reports a theological debate on the creation of human acts drawn from the phrase "He makes you travel", a debate the commentators do not settle.

This verse describes people who, after being rescued from the peril of the sea, having called on God sincerely and promised to be grateful, immediately turn to corruption and wrongdoing on earth without right. God then warns them that their transgression harms only themselves, that it is a fleeting enjoyment of the life of this world, and that they will return to Him to be informed of what they did. The commentators agree that baghy means transgression, oppression and corruption, that its harm falls back on the one who commits it, and that the closing announcement is a threat of requital. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note, citing a hadith, that such wrongdoing may be punished already in this world, while others do not develop the point. On the reading of matā', the majority take it in the nominative as a predicate, while Hafs reads it in the accusative, which opens several grammatical readings explored by Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi also observe that 'against yourselves' may mean against your own kind, so that people wrong one another. Al-Razi reads the shift from direct address to the third person as an expression of reproach, whereas Zamakhshari sees it as emphasis on the wonder at their conduct. Modern commentators such as Ibn 'Ashur distinguish unjust transgression from lawful force, and Sayyid Qutb stresses the certainty of divine accountability.

In this verse God likens the life of this world to rain sent down from the sky: the plants of the earth grow thick with it, people and livestock eat from them, and the earth takes on its adornment while its inhabitants think they control it. Then God's command arrives by night or by day and makes it stubble, as if it had not flourished the day before. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi agree on the main lesson: belittling worldly life and showing how quickly it vanishes, and warning that whoever clings to it is struck when he feels most secure. They also agree that the pronoun refers to the earth, meaning its vegetation. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi note that the phrase about the earth taking its ornaments is drawn from the image of a bride dressed in finery. On the meaning of 'ikhtalata bihi', al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari take it as the plants becoming intertwined, while al-Razi and al-Shawkani read the preposition as causal, and Abu Hayyan notes it can also mean accompaniment. For 'lam taghna', al-Tabari cites Qatada's reading as 'not enjoying', al-Mawardi records four interpretations, and al-Zamakhshari and others mention Marwan's reading. Commentators also differ on the reading of 'wazzayyanat', and al-Tabari reports an attributed variant he rejects as unreliable. Al-Razi lists several possible grounds for the comparison, from the owner's hope to resurrection. Ibn Sa'di praises the example as fitting the reality of the world, and the commentators close by urging reflection on the passing of worldly life.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the parable of vegetation that flourishes and then withers, and calls people to the lasting life to come. God invites His servants to His abode, which is Paradise, called the Abode of Peace because it is free from calamities, worries and sorrows. He guides whom He wills to the straight path, which most identify as Islam. The commentators agree that the Abode of Peace is Paradise, that the call is general to all people, while guidance is specific to those whom God wills. On why it is so named, opinions differ: Qatada and al-Hasan, as cited by Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, say that Peace is God and His abode is Paradise; al-Zajjaj, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi take it to mean safety from every affliction; others take it to refer to the greeting exchanged among the people of Paradise and the angels. As for the straight path, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi give four explanations: the Book of God, Islam, the truth, and what delivers one from error. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi use the verse in the debate over guidance and divine will, al-Razi distinguishing the general call from the particular guidance, while the Mu'tazilites, as al-Alusi reports, understand guidance as divine grace and support. Most cite the hadith of Jabir about the parable of the king and the feast as an explanation of this call. Ibn Kathir and others also note that the most widespread reading of the added good as the vision of God's face is the best known, though some offer other meanings.

This verse promises that those who did good, that is, who worshipped God with faith and obedience, will receive "the best reward", which is Paradise, along with "an increase". The commentators generally agree that the best reward is Paradise, but they differ on what the increase is. Abu Bakr, Hudhayfa, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Qatada, al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Layla, as reported by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, understand it as gazing upon the Face of God, citing the hadith of Suhayb related by Muslim. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Zayd and others, as al-Tabari records, take a different view. For Ibn Abbas, the best reward is a good deed repaid tenfold, and the increase is its multiplication up to seven hundred times. For Mujahid, the increase is forgiveness and divine pleasure, while for Ibn Zayd it is the provision given in this world for which they will not be held to account. Al-Zamakhshari also cites a report about a single pearl. Al-Razi favours the vision of God as the increase, whereas the Mu'tazilites read it as an extra grace beyond the reward. As for the rest of the verse, the commentators explain that no dust or humiliation will cover their faces, a meaning given by al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir. The verse ends by stating that they are the people of Paradise, where they will remain forever.

The commentators explain that this verse contrasts the fate of the wrongdoers with that of the doers of good just mentioned. It means that those who earned evil deeds, which most take to be associationism and sins, will be repaid with a punishment equal to their misdeed and no more. Humiliation will cover them, no one will protect them from God, and their faces will seem covered with pieces of the darkest night. They are the companions of the Fire, where they will remain forever. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take the 'evil deeds' here mainly to mean disbelief and associating partners with God, while others include all sins. The grammarians differ on the role of 'jaza'': al-Tabari supplies an understood 'for them', whereas al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya make it the subject with 'by its like' as predicate. Al-Tabari prefers the reading qit'an with a fatha, which most readers use, while Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read it with a sukun, meaning 'a portion of the night'. Al-Razi sees the darkness as a sign of ignorance, while Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it as blackness of the face, sorrow or humiliation. The Mu'tazilites cite the verse for the eternity of grave sinners, but al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi reply that it concerns unbelievers. Ibn Sa'di adds that the inner humiliation spreads to the outward appearance.

This verse depicts the Day of Resurrection, when all creatures are gathered. The idolaters and their objects of worship are ordered to stay in their places to be judged, then they are separated and the ties that bound them in this world are severed. The commentators agree that the worshipped beings disown their worshippers and that God calls Himself witness to their innocence. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari understand the "associates" as the idols, while Mujahid and others say God will make the idols speak. Al-Razi lists several possibilities: angels, devils, or anything worshipped besides God. Al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur also report that the idols are enabled to speak on that occasion. As for the phrase "it was not us that you worshipped", some say it means the worshippers followed their desires or their devils, while others say it reflects the idols' unawareness of the worship offered to them. Al-Razi and al-Alusi propose different explanations for why they lie in that state of bewilderment. The commentators finally link the passage to the moment when every soul tests what it has done and the false claims vanish before the true Lord.

This verse describes the scene of the Day of Resurrection: God gathers all people, then orders the polytheists and their associates to stay in their places so that a separation can take place, and the objects of worship disown those who worshipped them. The commentators differ on who the "associates" are. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi, al-Alusi and others understand them to be the idols, which God causes to speak. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir broaden the meaning to everything worshipped besides God. Al-Razi notes that they may be the angels, the idols, or others. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Mawardi include the angels and the Messiah. According to al-Tabari and Mujahid, the worshipped beings say they were unaware of the worship directed at them, and call God to witness. Al-Razi and al-Wahidi explain that they meant they had not commanded this worship and had not consented to it. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir take the heedlessness to mean complete lack of awareness, since they are inanimate. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi read it as a lack of approval. Al-Alusi also notes that the angels are not supposed to be unaware, and that the reference may include the devils who misled people, as Ibn 'Ashur reports. The commentators agree that the verse aims to rebuke the idolaters and to show the falsehood of what they worshipped. On that day each soul is tested by its past deeds, the idolaters return to God their true master, and what they used to invent vanishes from them. Ibn Kathir links this passage to the theme of judgment and the unveiling of truth.

The verse describes the Day of Judgment, when every soul is tested by what it sent forward of deeds, is returned to God, its true Master, and what the polytheists used to invent, namely the claim that their deities would intercede for them, vanishes. The commentators agree that this refers to the reckoning and recompense, and that returning to God means submitting to His just judgment. The phrase "their true Master" means the one who truly owns and governs their affairs, not a helper or supporter.

The readings differ on the verb. The majority reading "tabluu" with a single ba' means "to test"; Mujahid and al-Kalbi take it as testing or knowing, and al-Zajjaj as the soul coming to know the outcome of its deeds. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "tatlu" with two dots above: al-Sudi and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as "to follow" what the soul did, others as "to read" the record of one's deeds, and Ibn Zayd as "to witness." Al-Tabari holds that both readings are sound and close in meaning.

On the apparent conflict with the verse stating that the disbelievers have no protecting mawla, commentators explain that the word carries different senses: here owner and sovereign, there helper and supporter. Others, like Ibn Kathir, stress that all affairs return to God the Just. Finally, the deities that were worshipped disown their worshippers, and the fabrications disappear.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to ask the polytheists who provides for them from the sky and the earth, who controls their hearing and sight, who brings the living out of the dead and the dead out of the living, and who governs all affairs. The commentators explain that they will answer that it is Allah, so they should fear Allah by abandoning association with Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy agree that it is an argument from the lordship of God, which the polytheists accepted, to establish that worship belongs to Him alone. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi specify that provision from the sky is rain and from the earth is vegetation, and that bringing the living out of the dead includes the embryo from the drop, the bird from the egg and the plant from the seed. Al-Razi builds his argument in stages, from provision, then the senses, then life and death, and sees the general statement on governance as following the details. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari note that the particle 'min' indicates provision comes from both sources, and al-Zamakhshari sees the verse as a refutation of the Qadariyya. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes this passage from the one in Surat Saba: here 'sky' is singular because the listeners acknowledge rain falling from the clouds, while there the Prophet is told to answer himself. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that in matters of belief there is no middle position between truth and error, unlike in matters of law. On the phrase 'thus the word of your Lord has come true', most commentators take it to mean that God's decree is that the disbelievers will not believe, and al-Razi draws from it a detailed theological debate on predestination.

The commentators explain that this verse addresses the polytheists, who had already acknowledged that God grants sustenance, gives hearing and sight, brings the living out of the dead and the dead out of the living, and governs all affairs. God then says: that One is your Lord, the Truth; and what lies beyond the truth but error? How, then, are you turned away? Al-Tabari, al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi take the verse as a rebuke of associationism, since acknowledging Lordship entails worshipping God alone. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari note that in matters of belief there is no third position between truth and error, whereas legal questions admit differing opinions, a point al-Qurtubi also makes. Drawing on the verse, al-Qurtubi reports that Malik, Ibn Wahb and al-Zuhri disapproved of chess and backgammon, while al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa permitted them under certain conditions; Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi, however, hold that the verse concerns faith rather than practical rulings. On the phrase 'thus the word of your Lord has come true', al-Razi reads it as a divine decree of disbelief, a view rejected by al-Jubba'i, who relies on the passive verb 'turned away'; al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir understand it as the fixed judgement of God against the wicked. Al-Biqa'i, al-Shawkani and Abu al-Su'ud stress the clarity of the truth and the senselessness of turning away from it. The overall meaning that emerges is a warning against polytheism and a call to recognise that God's Lordship grounds His exclusive worship.

This verse states that the disbelief of the polytheists and their refusal to believe came about through God's prior decree. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the "word of your Lord" is His prior judgement and knowledge, and that those who "transgressed" are those who rebelled in their disbelief and left obedience. Al-Wahidi and al-Zamakhshari take it as a threat of punishment, with "they will not believe" being either an apposition to that word or its justification. Al-Samani notes, citing the exegetes, that the verse refers to particular people whom God knew would not believe.

The commentators agree on the general sense: those who persisted in refusal after the truth had been shown to them are judged by the divine word. They differ on what "thus" refers to. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Atiyya link it to the turning away from truth, to the preceding verdict, or to truth itself, while Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi link it to the lordship of God. Al-Razi draws from the verse an argument for predestination and answers al-Jubba'i, who read it as proof that God does not lead astray. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes the legal words of God from His creative words and places this verse among the latter.

On recitation, Nafi' and Ibn Amir read "words" in the plural, the others in the singular, which most commentators consider equivalent in meaning. Ibn Ashur also holds that the two readings have the same sense.

In this verse God orders His Prophet to ask the polytheists whether any of their associates can originate creation and then bring it back after it perishes. The expected answer is no, so the Prophet is told to answer on their behalf that God alone begins creation and restores it, and then to rebuke them for turning away from the truth. The commentators explain that resurrection is mentioned although the pagans deny it, because its proof is so clear that it is treated as settled, and denying it is stubbornness. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi understand the Prophet to answer in their place because their obstinacy prevents them from speaking the truth. Al-Alusi and al-Shinqiti hold instead that the verse specifies who performs these acts, and that the Prophet is not acting as their spokesman. Ibn 'Ashur sees the creation and resurrection as restricted to God alone, to the exclusion of associates. The following verses ask whether any associate guides to the truth, and the readings of the verb yahiddi gave rise to several interpretations: Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi take it as referring to the idols, al-Zamakhshari understands that an inert object moves only when it is carried, and al-Razi stresses the astonishment at the polytheists' misguidance. Al-Sha'rawi notes that the answer is known in advance and that the truth silences the opponent.

This verse asks the polytheists whether any of their associates can guide to the truth. The commentators agree that only God guides to the truth and that the idols guide no one. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the idolaters could not claim otherwise, since observation would refute them. On the phrase about one who is guided only if guided, Mujahid and al-Tabari take it to refer to idols, while al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi note that the wording treats them as rational beings. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari propose other readings: the target might be leaders of misguidance and callers to error, and the verb may mean being moved from place to place. The readings vary considerably. Al-Tabari prefers the most eloquent vocalisation, while Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan observe that the unvocalised form can mean seeking guidance. Several commentators, including al-Razi, draw from the verse that belief in matters of creed must rest on certainty rather than conjecture. The verse ends by affirming that God knows what they do, which serves as a warning.

This verse states that most of the polytheists follow nothing but conjecture in believing that the idols are gods and intercessors with God, and that conjecture can never replace the truth or benefit anyone in its place. God knows fully what they do, which is a warning to them. The commentators agree on this basic meaning but differ on who the word 'most' refers to. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir take it to mean all of them, while al-Mawardi and al-Wahidi take it to mean their leaders whom the common people follow. Al-Tabari understands conjecture as a doubt that cannot take the place of certainty, al-Mawardi describes it as a state between certainty and doubt, and Abu Hayyan sees it as empty imaginings and faulty analogies. Al-Razi judges that the stronger view is that the conjecture concerns the acknowledgment of God, since it rests on no proof, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi relate it to the claim that the idols are divine. Several scholars, including al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi, take from the verse that certainty is required in matters of belief and that blind imitation is not sufficient. Ibn 'Ashur notes, however, that conjecture remains valid in practical legal matters. Readings also differ on the final verb, with some reading the second-person form 'you do', as transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud.

This verse states that the Qur'an could not have been invented apart from God, that it confirms the earlier revealed Books such as the Torah and the Gospel, that it explains in detail what God has prescribed, and that there is no doubt about it because it comes from the Lord of the worlds. The commentators agree on its inimitability: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya stress that no human can produce its like, and Ibn Kathir adds that it corrects the distortions in earlier Scriptures. On the meaning of confirming what lies before it, al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi take it as confirmation of the earlier Books, while al-Mawardi and al-Sam'ani also mention the Resurrection and Judgment, or what those Books foretell. Al-Razi grounds the miracle in two things: its accounts of past and future events, and the breadth of religious knowledge it contains. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take the pronoun in 'there is no doubt in it' to refer to the Qur'an, while al-Alusi and Abu al-Su'ud discuss the grammar without settling it. The challenge to produce a similar sura is cited by all, but al-Razi sees it as a progression from ten suras to a single one, whereas Ibn Atiyya holds that it concerned eloquence and composition rather than unseen predictions. Al-Tabari and al-Jalalayn explain the phrase about denying what they had not grasped as a hasty rejection before examination, and al-Zamakhshari links it to clinging to the traditions of the ancestors. Al-Kalbi and Muqatil, reported by al-Baghawi, consider the verse abrogated by the verse of fighting. Ibn Sa'di draws the lesson that one should not accept or reject a matter before understanding it.

The verse reports the claim of the polytheists that the Prophet fabricated the Quran himself. God commands him to challenge them to produce a surah like it in eloquence and composition, and to call on whomever they can besides God, if they are truthful. The commentators agree that this challenge proves the Quran's inimitability and the inability of humans to match it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the pronoun "like it" refers to the Quran and that "surah" means any portion of it, even a short one. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi read it as a surah like one of the surahs of the Quran. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan propose an implied condition: if things are as you claim, produce such a text yourselves. Al-Razi lists six levels of the challenge, from the whole Quran down to a single surah with the help of others. The commentators also note that the Quran confirms earlier scriptures and that its narratives agree with the Torah and the Gospel, which al-Razi treats as evidence of its divine origin. As for why the people rejected it, al-Zamakhshari first attributes this to hasty denial and imitation of the fathers and then to obstinacy after reflection, while Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari point to ignorance. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi note that "ta'wil" may mean the outcome foretold, namely punishment. On the following verses, Ibn Kathir holds that "to me my deeds, to you yours" is a firm ruling, whereas Muqatil, al-Kalbi and Ibn Zayd consider it abrogated by the verse of fighting, a view the researchers reject.

This verse explains that the polytheists did not reject the Qur'an after careful examination; they called it a lie before grasping its meaning and before its ta'wil, meaning what its announcements would lead to, had come to pass. Commentators compare their conduct with that of earlier peoples toward their messengers, and urge the reader to consider how the wrongdoers ended. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Abu al-Su'ud agree that ta'wil here means the fulfilment of the threatened punishment, and that the wrongdoers are the peoples who rejected their messengers. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Razi understand that the denial came without reflection, which blames haste and blind imitation; al-Zamakhshari adds that the particle 'lamma' suggests an expectation that the Qur'an's inimitability would be shown. Ibn 'Atiyya allows both senses, the threat and the report of the unseen. Al-Razi lists several causes of the denial, including the strangeness of resurrection, the incomprehensible opening letters, and the gradual revelation. Al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy note that some of the addressees might believe inwardly or later embrace faith while others persist, and most conclude that God knows best who the corrupters are. Al-Baghawi and others regard the verse 'to me my deeds, to you yours' as abrogated by the verse of fighting, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi consider it not abrogated. Ibn Sa'di draws the lesson that one should verify before accepting or rejecting anything.

This verse states that among the people of the Prophet ﷺ some believe in the Qur'an and acknowledge that it comes from God, while others never believe in it or acknowledge it. God knows best the corrupters, meaning those who obstinately deny it, and the phrase is a warning to them. Commentators differ on the meaning. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir take the pronoun to refer to the Qur'an or the Prophet and the verb to refer to the future: some will believe later, while others will die in disbelief. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi hold that faith may be inward while denial is outward: some know the Qur'an is true yet stubbornly reject it, others deny out of ignorance or doubt. Ibn al-Jawzi reports, on the authority of Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, that the group meant is the Jews, while Muqatil identifies them as the Quraysh. Ibn Ashur links the verse to the previous one and compares this attitude to devotion to idols. As for the next verse, "If they call you a liar, say: my deeds are mine and yours are yours", al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Razi record that Ibn Zayd, Muqatil and al-Kalbi held it abrogated by the verse of fighting, though al-Razi finds this view unconvincing. Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur hold that it is not abrogated.

This verse instructs the Prophet that if the disbelievers persist in denying him after the proof has been presented, he should disown them and say: my deeds are mine and yours are yours, for each person is repaid for what he does and no one bears the burden of another's actions. Al-Tabari explains that the Prophet is not harmed by their deeds nor they by his, and he reports that Ibn Zayd held the verse abrogated by the command to fight. Al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Mujahid also considered it abrogated by the verse of the sword, as al-Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi repeat. Al-Mawardi, al-Sam'ani, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi, however, judge this abrogation weak, since the principle of individual responsibility does not contradict the verses on fighting. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read the verse as meaning that the Prophet has delivered his message and may now disown them, while Ibn Kathir sees in it an affirmation of God's justice. Ibn Ashur, al-Shinqiti and al-Qasimi regard the verse as muhkam, since disassociation from wrongdoing remains valid, and Ibn Ashur notes that the choice of the verb for action rather than a noun excludes every deed, present or future.

This passage describes some of the polytheists who listen to the Prophet ﷺ when he recites the Qur'an and teaches the laws, yet whose listening produces neither understanding nor acceptance: they are like the deaf who hear nothing. The question carries the sense of a negation: you cannot make the deaf hear, all the more so when reason is also absent. The parallel verse speaks of those who look at the Prophet and see the signs of his prophethood without believing, like the blind whom he cannot guide. Both verses console the Prophet: the failure of these people is not his fault, and guidance belongs to God alone.

The commentators agree that the deafness and blindness meant are of the heart and of insight, not of the ears or eyes, and that the listening described is that of hostility seeking flaws rather than seeking the truth. Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir note that this deprivation is not an injustice by God, and that people wrong themselves through disbelief and disobedience. Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud see here a statement that God has sealed their hearts so that no path to their faith remains, while Zamakhshari holds that guidance can only be granted by God, who alone has the power over it.

Opinions differ on who is meant: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Wahidi identify the mockers, such as al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Ibn al-Anbari identifies a group of Jews, and Ibn al-Jawzi records all three views, including Quraysh, without choosing. Razi discusses at length whether hearing or sight is superior, presenting arguments on each side without deciding. Zamakhshari notes that the verse separates those whose hatred is extreme from those who do not reach that degree.

This verse describes some of the disbelievers who look at the Prophet ﷺ and see the signs of his prophethood, yet do not believe or get guided, so they are like the blind. The commentators read it as consolation for the Prophet: he cannot guide someone whom God has deprived of success, just as he cannot give sight to a blind man. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the blindness as blindness of the heart, and say that God withheld tawfiq from them. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi stress discernment: a blind person with insight can still infer and reason, whereas someone who combines blindness with a lack of understanding cannot be guided. Al-Mawardi and al-Wahidi connect the verse to the preceding ones and read in it a note of astonishment. The next verse says God does not wrong people at all, but people wrong themselves. Al-Tabari takes this as meaning that the loss of guidance is a just punishment for earlier sins. Al-Razi reports the theological debate it raises: those who hold that God creates human acts see it as supporting their view, while the Mu'tazilites read it as proof that God compels no one. Al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi apply it to stubborn refusal. Ibn Qutayba cites the passage to prefer hearing over sight, which Ibn al-Anbari rejects, explaining that the reference is to blindness and deafness of the heart. Modern commentators such as Ibn 'Ashur and al-Sha'rawi link this blindness to hostility and to refusing to accept what one sees.

The commentators explain that this verse clears God of any injustice: He does not punish people, nor does He deprive them of their faculties or of the means of guidance, except as they have deserved it, and it is people who wrong themselves through disbelief and disobedience. Al-Tabari reads it as God's assurance to the Prophet and the believers that He did not take faith from these people without a prior offence on their part, but that the sins they had accumulated brought about this deprivation. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi stress that God is just and bountiful in all His acts. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi also suggest that the verse may be a warning: the punishment of the Last Day is fair, since the wrongdoers themselves brought about its causes. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud draw from it that the servant has a share of acquisition and is not stripped of choice entirely, against the view of the Jabriyya. Al-Razi reports that the Sunni scholars take the verse as proof that human acts are created by God, while the Mu'tazilites take it as proof that God compelled no one to evil. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the closing phrase serves as a conclusion with an allusion to punishment. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the particle with a light nun and al-nas in the nominative, while the other readers use the doubled nun and al-nas in the accusative.

The verse describes the Day when God gathers the disbelievers, who will feel they stayed only an hour of a day, so overwhelmed will they be, and who will recognise one another as they did in the world. It concludes that those who denied meeting God have lost, and that they were not guided. The commentators agree that loss here means the loss of the self and of the reward of Paradise, and that the sentence expresses wonder at their fate. They differ on the period meant: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi take it as the life of this world, while others, including Ibn Abbas, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi, take it as the stay in the graves, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya allow both. On the word ta'arruf, Ibn Abbas and al-Kalbi understand mutual recognition on leaving the graves, which the terror then ends, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy understand a recognition of reproach, in which each blames the other for leading him astray. Al-Dahhak restricts it to the mutual affection of believers. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir set this verse beside those saying no questions will pass between relatives, to show that recognition fades. Al-Razi compares this loss to a man who pays a fortune for glass he took for a jewel. Ibn Ashur sees the verse as a warning to those who denied the resurrection.

In this verse God tells His Prophet Muhammad that the punishment promised to the polytheists will certainly come. Either God will show him part of it during his lifetime, as at Badr where their leaders were killed and captured, or God will take him before that. In both cases all of them return to God, who knows their deeds and will repay them. The commentators agree that this return means judgment and punishment in the Hereafter, and that the 'witnessing' means its consequence, which is punishment, as al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi say that what was shown to the Prophet was the punishment of Badr, and the rest will come after death. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy hold that God showed His Prophet various forms of humiliation of the disbelievers in this world, and that what awaits them on the Day of Resurrection is greater. Ibn 'Ashur notes that 'then' marks a higher rank rather than a sequence in time, and he takes the main point to be the detailed threat of judgment. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Wahidi summarise the meaning as: if God does not take revenge on them quickly, He will take it later. Al-Sha'rawi and other modern commentators see the verse as a consolation to the Prophet. Some readings, mentioned by Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur, vary slightly in wording but not in meaning.

This verse states that God sent to every past community a messenger to call its people to the worship of the One God and to obedience. When the messenger came with his message and his people denied him, judgment was passed between them with justice: the messenger and those who followed him were saved, while the deniers were punished. No one is wronged in this, since each person's punishment follows from his own deeds. The commentators largely agree on this sense. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya first take it as a matter of the Hereafter, with Mujahid and Muqatil specifying that the messenger will come on the Day of Resurrection to bear witness against his people, and the judgment will then bring salvation to the believers and punishment to the disbelievers, as in the verse about the prophets and witnesses being brought forth and judgment passed between them. Al-Hasan, by contrast, places this judgment in this world, through punishment hastened upon the rebels, while al-Kalbi and Ibn al-Sa'ib locate it in the next life. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi see the closing phrase as emphasising God's perfect justice. Al-Qurtubi notes that another reading holds that peoples are not punished before a messenger is sent, a view also reflected in Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir. The verse is followed in its context by the unbelievers' question about when the promise will come, to which God replies that no community can advance or delay its appointed term.

This passage records the mocking, impatient question of the disbelievers: when will this promise come about, if you are truthful? Most commentators understand the promise to be the punishment with which the Prophet threatened them, while some take it to mean the Hour of Resurrection. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the question was a demand to hasten a punishment that had not yet been appointed. Al-Razi argues that the question cannot concern the hereafter, where the truth of promises is evident, and so it expresses denial or mockery. Al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi connect it to the announcement that Dieu would show the Prophet part of the punishment during his life. The next verse answers that the Prophet controls neither harm nor benefit for himself except as God wills, and that every community has a fixed term that it cannot advance or delay. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read the exception as disjunctive, meaning that what God wills is what will happen, while others allow it to be connected. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note a reading attributed to Ibn Sirin that puts the word for term in the plural. Ibn Abbas, cited by Ibn al-Jawzi, holds that the speakers were the earlier nations, whereas the more widely held view is that they were the Meccan polytheists. Ibn Ashur explains that the question expresses delay and denial, and that the reply addresses the Prophet and believers together. Ibn Sa'di and al-Qasimi stress that the appointed time belongs to God alone.

The verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to answer those who demand the punishment that he has no power over his own harm or benefit except what God wills, and that every community has a fixed term which it cannot delay or hasten by a moment once it arrives. Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that the Prophet does not know the unseen and cannot bring the punishment forward or postpone it, since it has an appointed time with God. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi read the exception as disjunctive, meaning that what God wills is what will happen, whereas al-Alusi notes that it may be read as connected, meaning except what God wills me to possess. Al-Razi also takes the exception as disjunctive, in answer to the Mu'tazilites. The commentators agree that the verse responds to the mocking impatience of the disbelievers and reassures the Prophet. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the Quraysh challenged the Prophet about the punishment, and that they will believe when it comes but that their faith will then be of no benefit. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya understand their question as denial or contempt. Ibn Sa'di and al-Alusi link the passage to the sending of a messenger to every community, whose judgment is made with justice.

God tells His Prophet to ask the polytheists who were demanding the punishment: if God's punishment comes upon you by night while you sleep, or by day while you are busy with your livelihood, what is it that the criminals wish to hasten? The commentators agree that this is a rhetorical question expressing denial and dread, since punishment is by nature repugnant and no one should seek it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya identify the criminals as the polytheists who mocked the Prophet and asked when the punishment would come. Most read the pronoun 'from it' as referring to the punishment, while az-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi allow that it may refer to God. They differ on the implied answer to the condition: al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi supply something like 'you would regret your haste or recognise your error'; az-Zamakhshari holds that the question itself serves as the answer, a view Abu Hayyan rejects because an interrogative answer needs the particle fa. All agree that their haste was a form of denial and mockery, so when the punishment falls they are told: do you believe now, when you were demanding it? Faith is then of no benefit, as Ibn Kathir supports with other verses. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that those told to taste the eternal punishment are those who wronged themselves through disbelief, not through mere disobedience.

The commentators explain that this verse rebukes the polytheists who demanded the punishment mockingly and in denial. God tells them that if punishment strikes them and they then believe, that faith will not benefit them, and they will be asked with reproach: do you believe now, when you were hastening it? Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi explain that the particle here means 'then, at that moment', used in a rebuking interrogative sense. Al-Tabari holds that this reading of 'thumma' is a fixed meaning, while Ibn 'Atiyya considers his claim unfounded and maintains that the sense is sound even if 'thumma' is read as the ordinary conjunction. Al-Zamakhshari suggests that the clause 'what the criminals seek to hasten' may serve as the conditional response or as a parenthetical, with the implied sense that they would regret their haste or recognize their error. Abu Hayyan rejects this view, noting that an interrogative clause cannot serve as a conditional response without a linking particle. On who speaks the word 'now', al-Qurtubi says it is the angels mocking them, while others take it to be God's own words. Most commentators refer the pronoun 'him' to the punishment, and some to God. Several scholars, including al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi, note that 'hastening' here really means denying, which makes the phrase stronger. Ibn Kathir compares the verse with the account of Pharaoh, whose faith at drowning was not accepted. Some readers, including Nafi', read 'alan' with the hamza dropped.

This verse describes those who wronged themselves by disbelief. They are told on the Day of Judgment to taste the everlasting punishment, and then they are reproached with a question implying that they are repaid only for what they earned. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi, understand the wrong as associating partners with God, and the earning as disbelief, denial and sins. Al-Qurtubi says the words are spoken by the keepers of Hell. Al-Razi draws three lessons: the question aims at humiliation, reward follows deeds, and the verse shows that the servant acquires his actions. He reports that the Mu'tazilites take this as proof that good deeds earn a due reward from God, that the People of the Sunna read it as a pure promise, and that the Jabriyya deny that the servant acquires anything. The commentators do not settle this dispute. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud link the verse to the earlier passage on those who hurried the punishment, since faith does not help once it has come, as al-Baghawi and Ibn Atiyya explain. The passage then turns to the question of the disbelievers about whether the promise is true, to which the Prophet answers with an oath that it is true and that they cannot escape God, as al-Tabari and al-Mawardi note. Commentators draw no particular legal ruling from this verse and focus on its meaning, grammar and warning.

The disbelievers ask the Prophet ﷺ, mockingly or incredulously, whether what they are threatened with is true. God commands him to answer with an oath: yes, by my Lord, it is true beyond doubt, and you cannot escape it. The commentators agree that the 'truth' refers to the punishment, the resurrection and the warning of the Quran. Al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi state it means the resurrection or the punishment of the afterlife, while Ibn Kathir understands it as resurrection after the bodies turn to dust. For 'you cannot escape it', al-Mawardi cites Ibn Abbas, who reads it as 'you cannot outrun it', while al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi take it as 'you will not flee the punishment'. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud note that reading 'al-haqq' with the definite article hints that their claim is false and so is ironic. Ibn Atiyya leans toward the sense of a warning. Al-Razi considers the question vain since it was already answered, and sees the oath as raising the matter to seriousness, like the Bedouin who was satisfied with an oath. Al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi explain that 'iy' means 'yes' and is used only with an oath. Ibn Ashur sees the answer as a wise reply that turns their question back on them. All agree the statement is an emphatic affirmation of the reality of the coming punishment.

This verse depicts the terror of the Day of Judgment and the fate of wrongdoers. God states that if every soul that did wrong owned everything on earth, it would offer it as ransom to escape punishment, but it would not be accepted. Most commentators understand wrong-doing here as associating partners with God, and ransom as giving up what might save one from punishment. On the phrase 'they will conceal their remorse', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Jalalayn explain that they hide their regret. Al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi and al-Sam'ani add that the leaders concealed it from their followers out of fear of their reproach. Abu 'Ubayda, al-Mubarrad, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi hold that it means they openly showed their remorse, since that day is no place for feigned patience. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi mention further meanings: sincere repentance, or being so stunned by the sight of punishment that they cannot speak, like a condemned man led to the gallows. On 'judged between them with justice', al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take it to mean between wrongdoers and the wronged, al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi between leaders and followers, and al-Razi between believers and disbelievers. All agree that God does not wrong anyone and punishes only for one's own deeds. The verse then affirms that the dominion of the heavens and earth belongs to God, that His promise is true, and that most people do not know it.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God alone, and that His promise, whether of reward or punishment, is true and cannot be broken. Many connect it to what precedes it: a wrongdoer owns nothing he could offer as ransom, since all dominion belongs to God. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya take the promise to cover both reward and punishment, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur also see in it the resurrection. The phrase "but most of them do not know" refers, according to al-Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi, to the polytheists; al-Razi attributes their ignorance to their heedlessness of the proofs, while al-Baydawi ties it to the weakness of their minds, which see only the life of this world. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that limiting the ignorance to "most" implies that some people believe and therefore know. Al-Razi and al-Alusi read the opening "alā" as a call to awaken the heedless. The ambiguity of the verb "asarru" (to conceal or to display regret) is noted by al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya, each favouring a reading.

This part of the verse affirms that God alone gives life and causes death, and that all people will be returned to Him. Al-Tabari explains that God is never unable to revive the polytheists after death or to cause them to die when He wills, and that they will return to Him to witness what they had denied, namely His threat and punishment. The commentators agree on the plain meaning; al-Sam'ani simply calls it clear. Al-Jalalayn and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the return means recompense for deeds, and Abu al-Su'ud adds that giving life and death happen in this world without anyone sharing in them. Al-Alusi holds that this points to the resurrection: a God who is powerful in His essence never loses that power, and the matter capable of life and death is capable of both forever. Al-Razi links the verse to the argument earlier in the surah: the One who created at first can create again. Al-Nasafi and al-Qasimi describe the return as the reckoning and judgement, which should produce both fear and hope. Ibn Kathir stresses God's knowledge of scattered bodies and His power to gather them. The commentators do not differ on the core meaning; they differ only on whether the return is best understood as judgement or as resurrection.

God addresses all of humanity: the Quran has come to them as an admonition from their Lord, a reminder of divine punishment and a warning against His threat, a cure for what is in the chests, namely ignorance, doubt and corrupt beliefs, a guidance that distinguishes truth from falsehood, and a mercy for the believers who benefit from it. The commentators agree that the admonition calls to good and restrains from evil, that the healing concerns the diseases of the heart, and that guidance is the clear proof leading to truth. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim extend the healing to both doubts and desires. All agree that mercy is reserved for believers, the only ones who profit from it. The disagreement concerns the meaning of 'grace' and 'mercy' in the following verse. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Hasan and Mujahid take grace to be Islam and mercy the Quran, while al-Dahhak and Zayd ibn Aslam reverse this, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri takes grace to be the Quran and mercy to be being counted among its people, and Ibn 'Umar takes grace to be Islam and mercy its adornment in the heart. Ibn 'Atiyya considers it better to take both words in a general sense without restriction. On the reading of the verb of rejoicing, most read the third person, while others read the second person, which Ibn 'Atiyya regards as a rare usage. All agree that the joy commanded is joy in God's grace and mercy, not in the passing goods of this world.

God commands His Prophet to tell people that true joy should come from God's grace and mercy, that is, from the Qur'an, the guidance and Islam that have reached them, and that this is better than the wealth they gather in this world. The commentators agree that grace and mercy refer to Islam and the Qur'an, but they differ on which is which. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and Hilal ibn Yasaf hold that grace is Islam and mercy is the Qur'an, while Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Dahhak take the reverse view, and Mujahid holds that grace is faith and mercy is the Qur'an. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others also report that mercy has been understood as Paradise, protection from sin, or divine success. As for the verb "fal-yafrahu", most readers use the third person, while Ubayy ibn Ka'b and others read the second person; al-Tabari prefers the common reading as more faithful to Arabic usage. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim explain that the joy condemned in the Qur'an is joy in worldly possessions, whereas joy in God's grace is praiseworthy, and Ibn 'Atiyya adds that joy restricted to something good is not blameworthy. The commentators conclude that the full meaning rests with God.

The verse rebukes the polytheists who declared some of the provision Allah gave them forbidden and some lawful on their own authority, and asks them whether Allah permitted this or whether they are inventing lies against Him. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the reference is to practices such as the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila and the ham, and to the portions of crops and livestock they set aside for their idols. Ibn Kathir quotes a hadith narrated through Awf ibn Malik stating that what Allah gives a servant is lawful. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd link the verse to the earlier Quranic description of the share the Arabs assigned to God from their produce and cattle, and to their claim that what is in the wombs of certain animals belongs to the males alone. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud read the questions as a demand for confirmation, with am as a connective, while al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi take them as a rebuke, with am meaning rather. The verse closes with a warning to those who fabricate lies against Allah on the Day of Judgment, and with a reminder of His favour toward mankind, though most do not give thanks, according to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take the verse to show that the authority to make things lawful or unlawful belongs to Allah, al-Qurtubi also discussing whether it rules out reasoning by analogy. Ibn Sa'di concludes that the default ruling on foods is permissibility, except what the law forbids.

The commentators explain that this verse follows a rebuke of those who declare some provisions forbidden and others lawful without divine permission, as the pagans did with the baḥīra and sā'iba camels. Its plain meaning is that those who invent such lies against God should not imagine they will escape accountability on the Day of Resurrection, and that the fitting expectation for them is punishment. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Abu al-Su'ud explain God's grace (fadl) here as His deferring punishment in this world and granting the liars respite. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi instead read it as the blessings God bestowed: reason, the sending of messengers and the revelation of books. Ibn Kathir adds that it may also cover the permission of lawful goods in this world. On the phrase "most of them do not give thanks", the commentators largely agree it describes general ingratitude: al-Tabari takes it as failing to thank God for all His favours, al-Wahidi as failing to affirm God's oneness and obey Him, and Ibn 'Atiyya as any shortcoming in gratitude. Al-Jaza'iri and al-Sha'rawi stress the gravity of lying against God. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi observe that the question is a rhetorical warning meant to startle the polytheists out of their heedlessness.

This verse states that God observes every circumstance of the Prophet and every deed of people, and that nothing escapes His knowledge, not even something as small as an atom's weight on earth or in heaven. Commentators agree on this general meaning. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others explain «you engage in it» (tufidun fihi) as «you act upon it» or «you undertake it», an interpretation al-Tabari adopts. Al-Dahhak instead understands it as spreading falsehood about the Quran, a view al-Tabari does not favour. The verb «ya'zubu» means to be absent or far away; al-Kisa'i reads it with a kasra, while most readers use a damma, and al-Tabari considers both forms correct.

The readings of «nor smaller nor greater» also differ. Most readers give it a fatha, coordinating it with «dharra», whereas Hamza and Ya'qub read it with a raf', as al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain by coordination with the grammatical position of the earlier word or by treating it as a new sentence. Al-Tabari prefers the fatha. The commentators agree that the «Clear Book» is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), as reported from Ibn 'Abbas and cited by al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir. Ibn Kathir links the verse to the hadith of excellence (ihsan), in which one worships God as if seeing Him. The passage contains no legal rulings; its purpose is to affirm the comprehensiveness of divine knowledge, and several scholars use it to answer those who doubt that God knows particulars.

This verse states that the friends of God, meaning those close to Him and worthy of His protection, will have no fear and no sorrow. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, the fear concerns what lies ahead in the afterlife and the sorrow concerns what they lost in this world. The commentators agree that the verse is then defined by what follows: they are those who believed and were god-fearing, as Ibn Abbas, al-Mawardi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Ashur explain. Some, such as al-Sam'ani and al-Tha'alibi, add outward signs, such as believers whose sight reminds people of God, or those who love one another for God's sake. These reports are cited by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Suyuti, and their reliability is discussed. Al-Razi and al-Alusi describe closeness to God as a closeness of the heart, while al-Qasimi stresses that faith and piety are indispensable, and others see divine support in that closeness. On the nature of fear and sorrow, al-Razi holds that fear concerns the future and sorrow the past, so the verse mainly refers to the afterlife, though al-Alusi notes that the negation does not exclude trials in this life. Ibn Ashur explains that the negation is strong and lasting, without denying passing emotions. As for the good news promised in this life, most cite the good dream, one that the believer sees or is shown, reported from Abu Hurayra, Ubada ibn al-Samit and Abu al-Darda, while al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Dahhak connect it to the angels at death or to Quranic promises. In the afterlife it is Paradise according to Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and others, and the welcome of the angels. Finally, the phrase that there is no change to God's words means that He never breaks His promises, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir point out.

This verse describes the awliya' of God, namely those who believe and are mindful of God. They have no fear and no sorrow, and they receive good tidings both in this world and in the next. The commentators broadly agree that faith and piety are the conditions of being a friend of God: one who believes in God, His Messenger and what he brought, and who fulfils the obligations and avoids what is forbidden. Opinions differ on the good tidings of this world. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Ashur relay, through hadiths attributed to the Prophet transmitted by Ubada ibn al-Samit and Abu al-Darda', that it is the true dream seen by the believer or shown to him. Qatada, al-Dahhak and al-Zuhri understand it as the announcement the angels make to the believer at death, al-Hasan as what God promised in the Quran, and others, such as al-Razi, include people's love and praise. As for the good tidings of the Hereafter, most cite Paradise, while Ibn 'Abbas links them to God's pleasure at the moment of death. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi also discuss the phrase that there is no change in God's words, which guarantees the fulfilment of His promise. Several authors cite hadiths about those who love one another for God's sake and about those whose sight reminds people of God. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the absence of fear may concern worldly life without meaning the total absence of anxiety, whereas most exegetes apply it to the Hereafter.

This verse states that the friends of God, namely those who believe and are mindful of Him, receive good news both in this life and in the Hereafter, that the words of God cannot be changed, and that this is the great triumph. Commentators agree that the good news of the Hereafter is Paradise and God's pleasure, and that God's promise admits no exception. On the good news of this world, opinions differ. Abu al-Darda', Ubada ibn al-Samit and Abu Hurayra, as transmitted by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, identify it as the true dream that a believer sees or that is shown to him, a view also adopted by al-Qurtubi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan. Qatada, al-Zuhri and al-Dahhak take it to be the glad tidings that reach the believer at the moment of death, or his knowledge of his place in Paradise before he dies. Al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan understand it as God's promises in the Book concerning Paradise and His generous reward. Al-Tabari judges it best to include all these meanings, since the verse encompasses them. Other reports mention people's love and a good reputation, related from Abu Dharr and cited by al-Mawardi, al-Razi and al-Baydawi. As for fear and sorrow, most commentators place them in the Hereafter, while Ibn 'Ashur understands that God guarantees His friends safety in both abodes. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that the verse defines God's friend by faith and piety.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ not to be grieved by the words of the disbelievers, whether their denial, their threats, or their plotting to undo his mission, and it gives the reason: all might and dominance belong to God alone, so no one possesses any share of it, and He will overcome his enemies and grant him victory. The commentators agree that the verse is a consolation and a promise of support. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that 'izza here means power and victory, and that God is the Avenger against the idolaters. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir note that the strength of the Prophet and the believers comes from God, so all of it belongs to Him, citing the verse 'Might belongs to God, to His Messenger and to the believers'. The readings and grammar differ over whether 'inna' is pronounced with a kasra or a fatha: most exegetes treat it as an independent explanatory clause, while Ibn Qutayba and al-Qadi held that reading it with a fatha, making the clause an appositive to 'their words', is a serious error bordering on disbelief. Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur reject that verdict and accept the fatha reading as valid when understood as a causal explanation. Al-Razi observes that a person grieves over a threat only if he believes it can harm him, so one who knows that it cannot harm him is no longer grieved. The commentators conclude that God is 'the All-Hearing' of their words and 'the All-Knowing' of their intentions, and that He will repay them, which is itself a warning to them.

This verse states that everything in the heavens and on earth belongs to God, as His creatures and possessions, so none of them can deserve lordship or be His partner. Those who call on other than God, therefore, are not following real partners, but only conjecture, and they are merely guessing and lying. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, understand the partners as the idols and objects the polytheists worshipped, which they believed would intercede for them or bring them closer to God, and they take the word conjecture to mean that their belief rests on assumption rather than certainty. The verse also comforts the Prophet, so that the words of the disbelievers do not grieve him, since all power belongs to God. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari explain that the word for those in the heavens and on earth refers to rational beings, angels, humans and jinn, and that mentioning them implies that inanimate things are even more subject to God. Ibn 'Ashur, however, sees the inclusion of inanimate beings as following the polytheists' own view that their idols were rational. On the particle ma, most take it as a negation, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan allow that it may be interrogative, expressing contempt and rebuke. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya consider the reading with the second person (tad'un) weak, whereas al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud find it meaningful as a rebuke to the polytheists for not following the example of the angels and prophets.

This verse states that God made the night for people to rest in and made the day bright so that they can see and pursue their livelihood, and that in this there are signs proving that He alone deserves worship, signs understood by those who listen with reflection. The commentators agree on this basic meaning. They differ on how to read the attribution of seeing to the day. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan take it as a metaphor, since the day is the place where one sees rather than the one who sees, and they cite Jarir's line about the night of the riding beasts not sleeping. Qutrub explains that the day becomes bright and seeing in the literal sense of the phrase. Ibn Kathir keeps the meaning of bright or illuminating. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur identify a rhetorical device called ihtibak, in which each half of the contrast implies the other: darkness for rest at night, light for activity by day. Al-Razi adds that the word seeing names the cause by its effect. As for those who listen, most commentators take this as listening that involves reflection and lesson-learning rather than mere hearing, as al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud state, and al-Razi emphasises pondering what they hear.

The verse reports the claim of the idolaters that God has taken a son, namely that the angels are his daughters, and God declares Himself exalted above such a thing. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the phrase 'Glory be to Him' is a declaration of His transcendence, and that He is the Self-Sufficient, to whom belongs all that is in the heavens and on earth. How could He have a son from among His own creatures? The commentators agree that a son presupposes need, whereas God has none.

Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan suggest the speakers could be worshippers of angels or idols, or Christians who speak of divine sonship, while Ibn Ashur argues that since the surah is Meccan, the address targets the polytheists rather than the People of the Book. Al-Zamakhshari extends the verdict to anyone who attributes a son to God. Al-Razi offers a series of arguments showing that the absolutely self-sufficient God cannot have a son: a son is part of his father, he helps his father, and he replaces a mortal parent. Ibn Ashur adds that taking a son springs either from desire or from a need for help or succession, both incompatible with divinity.

The word sultan is explained by Ibn Kathir and al-Qasimi as proof or argument, and al-Qasimi notes that the Quran uses the term for rational evidence. Grammarians differ on the attachment of bihadha: al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan connect it to the sense of presence in 'with you', while Abu al-Baqa connects it to sultan. The verse closes with a rebuke: 'Do you speak against God what you do not know?' Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan take this to mean that every claim without proof is ignorance and that beliefs require certain proof, and some draw from it a rejection of blind imitation in creed. Al-Alusi, however, denies that the verse can be used against analogy and single reports, since those matters belong to practical rulings.

This verse states that those who invent lies against God, such as attributing a son or a partner to Him, will not succeed, meaning they will not be saved from the Fire nor admitted to Paradise, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain. Most commentators understand 'falah' as salvation, success or lasting, and al-Tabari says it means they will not remain in this world, while Ibn al-Jawzi lists three views: they will not endure in this life, they will not be happy in the end, or they will not win. Al-Sam'ani and al-Kalbi take it to mean they will not be saved or will not believe. Al-Razi widens the verse to cover anyone who speaks about God and His attributes without knowledge or proof, and argues that one who thinks he has succeeded by gaining a quick worldly pleasure is deceived. All agree that the enjoyment they have in this world is small and temporary, before their return to God and the severe punishment for their disbelief. Grammarians differ on the word 'mata'', with al-Kisa'i reading it as 'that is an enjoyment' and al-Akhfash as 'they have an enjoyment'. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain it as a brief worldly benefit by which they keep their leadership in disbelief, and Ibn 'Ashur sees it as a small gain that will vanish.

This verse says that those who invent lies against God, such as attributing a son or partners to Him, will not prosper. What they gain in this world is only a brief and passing enjoyment; then they will return to God and suffer a severe punishment for their disbelief.

The commentators agree on the central meaning: enjoying wealth, status or comfort in this world does not count as success. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that this enjoyment lasts until the appointed term, while al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti specify that the punishment comes after death. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy identify the worldly gain with the leadership they keep through disbelief and their opposition to the Prophet. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Ashur explain that not prospering means failing to reach one's goal, and al-Razi adds that the warning covers anyone who speaks about God without knowledge.

They differ on when the punishment falls. Ibn Kathir places the return on the Day of Resurrection, whereas Abu al-Su'ud and al-Baydawi describe it as lasting misery. Abu Hayyan notes that the verse applies to those who attribute a son to God and to anyone who speaks of Him without proof.

Grammarians also differ. Al-Kisa'i takes mataʿ as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning that is or it is, while al-Akhfash reads it as there is an enjoyment for them. Al-Qurtubi reports both views.

God instructs His Prophet to recite to his contemporaries the story of Noah, who told his people that if his staying among them and his reminding them of God's signs weighed heavily upon them, he trusted in God alone. He then challenged them to unite their resolve with their associates, to make their scheme public rather than hidden, and to carry it out without delay. The commentators agree that Noah was confident in God's support and fearless of their plots, and that his words are a challenge and a consolation for the Prophet Muhammad. They differ on several points. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj read the waw in "and your associates" as meaning "together with", while others supply a hidden verb, "and call upon your associates", and al-Tabari backs the reading that attaches the word to the verb. Most identify the associates with the idols, al-Zamakhshari reading the phrase as mockery, while Ibn Kathir extends it to whatever is worshipped besides God. On the word ghumma, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Qutayba and al-Zajjaj take it as concealment or ambiguity, whereas Qatada, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir take it as distress or oppression. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand "iqdu ilayya" as "carry out what you intend", while others understand it as "inflict upon me the harm you plan". Al-Tha'alibi and al-Baghawi note the sense of a challenge that exposes the powerlessness of their gods. These variations do not change the central message of Noah's unshaken trust in God in the face of a hostile people.

God relates Noah's words to his people: if you turn away after the message has reached you, it is not because I asked you for any wage or reward; my recompense rests with God alone, and I have been commanded to be among those who submit. The commentators agree on the plain meaning: Noah disclaims any worldly motive and affirms the sincerity of his call. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi stress that he sought no payment and that his reward lies with God. Al-Mawardi and al-Zamakhshari note that a call free of greed carries more weight with hearts, and al-Razi sees in it a sign that Noah did not fear losing any benefit from them. On the meaning of submission, al-Tabari, al-Sam'ani and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as monotheism and obedience to God's command, while Ibn Kathir explains that it is the religion shared by all prophets even though their laws differ. Al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi draw from the verse that taking a fee for teaching religion is prohibited, whereas other commentators do not make this a ruling. Ibn 'Ashur observes that denying any wage reinforces the claim of disinterest, and al-Sha'rawi compares how the prophets spoke of wages, noting that Noah looks to the Lord alone for his reward.

The verse tells how the people of Nuh went on rejecting him after he had warned them, so God saved Nuh and those with him in the ark, made them successors on earth, and drowned those who denied His signs. It then tells the Prophet to look at the fate of those who had been warned. The commentators agree on the general meaning: the believers were saved and the deniers perished in the flood. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn Juzayy explain the word khala'if as those who replaced the drowned people as inhabitants of the earth. Ibn Kathir adds that those in the ark were the ones who followed Nuh's religion, and al-Sam'ani says they succeeded the drowned people in their homes and dwellings. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud state that there were eighty people in the ark, while al-Alusi reports forty men and forty women, noting that other figures are also given. Ibn Atiyya concludes from the verse that the flood reached only the people of a particular region rather than the whole earth, supporting this with the Prophet's hadith about the five things given to him. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Sa'di and al-Qasimi see the story as a warning to the disbelievers and a consolation for the Prophet. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi read the command to look as addressed to every listener, while al-Sha'rawi reads it as addressed first to the Prophet and then to his community. Al-Qurtubi and the Tafsir al-Jalalayn keep to the plain meaning.

This verse says that after Noah God sent many messengers to their peoples, who brought them clear proofs, yet these peoples did not believe in what they had earlier denied. The commentators explain that the sealing (tab') upon the hearts means that the heart is shut so it cannot accept guidance, and that the transgressors (mu'tadun) are those who exceed the limits in disbelief. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi take the sealing literally as the closing of the heart, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan treat it as an image for stubbornness, which is followed by divine abandonment.

The commentators agree that the messengers include Hud, Salih, Ibrahim, Lut and Shu'ayb, or others not named, each sent to his own people. They also agree that the negation with the particle of denial signals that faith was, for them, impossible because of their fierce obstinacy. They differ, however, on who the pronouns refer to: most link them to the peoples of the messengers, while Ibn 'Atiyya reports that some scholars link them to the people of Noah. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also mention a view that the earlier denial took place on the Day of the Covenant, when some denied in their hearts.

Al-Razi reports that Sunni scholars take this verse as evidence that God may prevent a person from believing, whereas the judge answers that sealing does not prevent faith. Ibn Kathir uses the passage as a warning to the Arab polytheists: if those who denied the earlier messengers were struck, how much more will those who denied the seal of the prophets face.

This verse states that after the messengers who came after Noah, God sent Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh and his chiefs with clear signs, yet they grew arrogant and refused, for they were a people of criminals.
