The commentators agree that the signs are miracles and proofs, and that the chiefs (al-mala') are the nobles and leaders who guide their people. Arrogance means claiming greatness and refusing to submit to the call. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di describe their crime as denial, stubbornness and corruption of God's servants, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that the greatest pride is to scorn the message of one's Lord once it has become clear.

Al-Tabari and al-Mawardi, among others, identify the messengers mentioned at the start as those who came after Noah, and the phrase "before" refers to the denial of earlier nations. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the pronoun in "they were" may refer to Noah's people or to all the messengers' peoples. Al-Tabari explains that the sealing of hearts is a punishment God imposes on those who transgress.

Regarding Pharaoh, al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Baydawi note that their claim that this was clear magic was a form of obstinacy, since they knew the truth is not magic. Grammarians have debated the question "Is this magic?": some take it as the words of Pharaoh's people, while Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan take it as Moses rebuking them. Al-Zamakhshari also explains that "to turn us away" means to divert us, and most exegetes take "greatness" to mean kingship.

This verse reports that when the truth that God sent through Moses and Aaron came to Pharaoh and his chiefs in the form of signs, they refused to submit and called it plain sorcery. The commentators agree that "the truth" means the miracles, such as the staff and the hand, that this was said when those signs were witnessed and confronted, and that it was the fruit of their arrogance and criminal conduct. The main disagreement concerns the grammar of the question "Is this sorcery?" Al-Tabari holds that these words are Moses' own, who omitted the first answer and let the second stand for it, and this is also the view of Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi. Al-Akhfash, by contrast, takes the words as a quotation of Pharaoh's people, while others read the question as an expression of wonder or admiration, as one would say of a horse that runs superbly. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan also suggest other readings, such as "do you blame and slander the truth?" Some readers recite the question with an interrogative alif, while the majority recite it as a statement. The phrase "magicians do not prosper" serves as proof, since if the signs were magic the sorcerer would not have prevailed. Al-Razi notes that turning the staff into a serpent or splitting the sea cannot be illusion. The early scholars also explain that "to turn us away" means to divert us, that "greatness" means kingship and rule over the land, and that "we will not believe you" means we will not trust you.

The commentators explain that after Pharaoh and his chiefs called the truth that had come from God sorcery, Moses rebuked them with a question of denial and reproach: is this sorcery? He then concludes that sorcerers do not prosper. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi agree that 'the truth' refers to the signs Moses brought, that the object of 'do you say' is implied and points back to their own words, and that the question is one of denial. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi propose that the verb means to blame or disparage, so that the sense is: do you find fault with the truth? Al-Farra' and the Kufan grammarians, followed by Ibn al-Anbari, read the interrogative alif as expressing admiration or amazement, while al-Tabari links it to a quotation of their own words. Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur note that the final clause may be Moses' own words or a quotation of his opponents' argument, and that it warns against using magic to win. Al-Tabari explains that sorcerers do not prosper and do not endure, while Ibn 'Ashur ties the point to the nature of magic itself. The commentators note some variant readings, including one that reads the question as an interrogative. They do not always settle these readings, but all of them agree that what Moses brought was not magic.

This verse records the reply of Pharaoh and his chiefs to Moses and Aaron: you have come to turn us away from the religion of our fathers, so that you may gain greatness and rule in the land of Egypt, and we will not believe you. The commentators explain talfitana as turning someone aside or twisting him away from something, as Qatada, Ibn Qutayba and al-Samani say, and they take this to mean worship of idols or the ancestral religion, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir state. Most of them understand al-kibriya' as kingship and authority, a view reported from Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Ibn Abbas, while al-A'mash takes it as majesty and Ibn Zayd as high station. Al-Tabari judges these meanings close to one another, since kingship is a form of authority and obedience a form of kingship. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy explain that kingship was called greatness because it is the highest thing sought in this world, and that kings are described as proud. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that the speakers give two reasons for refusing: blind imitation of their fathers and the desire to keep leadership. Al-Baydawi also suggests they may be insulting Moses and Aaron by implying they would become tyrants if they ruled, as the Copt said in another passage. Some readers, including Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan, read yakun in the third person. The closing phrase means they will not accept what the two brothers bring as true.

God tells us that Pharaoh ordered his attendants to bring every skilled magician, so that he could pit them against what Moses had brought. The commentators agree that Pharaoh summoned the magicians to confront Moses after seeing the staff and the white hand, which he took to be sorcery, as al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and al-Shawkani report. Ibn Kathir and al-Sam'ani mention how large the gathering was, with some saying there were seventy thousand magicians, and that Pharaoh hoped to defeat the truth through deception. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read the word as the intensive form "sahhar", while the majority read "sahir", a reading noted by Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that the phrase "when the magicians came" implies an omitted step, namely that they were brought, and that Moses told them to begin by casting what they had. Al-Tabari also identifies another omission that the context makes clear. Ibn 'Ashur holds that Pharaoh chose the most accomplished magicians to make the contest more forceful. The disagreements concern mainly recitation and grammatical construction rather than the overall meaning.

The commentators explain that Pharaoh ordered that every learned sorcerer be brought, and when the magicians arrived, Moses said to them: throw down what you are about to throw. Most exegetes see the verse as the moment of challenge, just before the magic takes effect, and Moses invites them to begin so that the falsehood of their craft becomes visible to all. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the magicians had been the ones to offer to go first, and al-Tabari notes that the text implies they then threw their ropes and staffs. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi add that this command does not mean Moses approved of sorcery, but meant to expose its emptiness. The reading of the word ma differs among scholars. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan explain that it can be relative or interrogative: in the reading of Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far, the interrogative form reproaches the magicians, while the common reading means that what you have brought is sorcery and not a sign from God. Al-Sha'rawi observes that the Quran gives only the essential moment here, with the other details found in other surahs.

Most commentators explain that when the magicians threw down their ropes and staffs, Moses told them that what they had brought was sorcery and not signs from God, and that God would nullify it, since God does not make the work of the corrupters endure. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur explain that this nullification came through Moses' miracle, when his staff swallowed what they had made. Al-Tabari, who reads the word as a statement rather than a question, holds that Moses did not doubt the nature of their magic, while others such as Abu 'Amr, Mujahid and Abu Ja'far read it as an interrogative. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take that question as a rebuke or a reproach, whereas al-Razi and al-Qurtubi see it as belittling or exaggerated.

The scholars also differ on the grammar. Al-Farra' and al-Razi attribute the definite article to the repetition of a previously indefinite noun, while Ibn 'Atiyya sees it as referring to a known matter. Abu Hayyan rejects this and argues that the word means something different in the two places. Al-Zamakhshari also notes that the Qur'an may report the words of opponents in other terms.

For the final phrase, al-Tabari understands that God does not support the deeds of those who do evil on earth. Al-Wahidi and al-Nasafi say that God does not make their work beneficial or lasting. Al-Alusi adds a nuance, noting that some forms of magic have a real effect, and that the verse mainly targets illusion and deception.

The commentators explain that after the magicians threw down their ropes and staffs, Moses told them that what they had brought was magic, that God would bring it to nothing, and that God does not set right the work of corrupters. He then said that God establishes the truth by His words, meaning by His command, decree and promise, even if the criminals dislike it. The exegetes agree that the words refer to God's command and decree, and a variant reading in the singular is also recorded.

Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan note that these words were spoken in the confrontation with Pharaoh, who had gathered the magicians at his request. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi observe that the closing sentence may be Moses' own words or a statement from God, and Ibn 'Atiyya inclines to the first view. Ibn 'Ashur explains that announcing the defeat of magic was meant to strike fear into the onlookers.

Opinions differ on the reading. Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read the opening word as a question, while most readers read it as a statement. Al-Zamakhshari takes the question as a rebuke, whereas al-Razi holds that the magic mentioned here is not the magic of which Moses was accused. As for the criminals, al-Tabari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take them to be Pharaoh's people or anyone guilty of wrongdoing, while Ibn 'Ashur sees them mainly as Pharaoh and his court.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the situation of Moses' people after his miracles and his triumph over the magicians: only a small number of young people, the descendants, believed in him, and they did so while fearing Pharaoh and the leading men of his people, who might turn them from their faith through torture. The verse adds that Pharaoh was a tyrant who dominated the land of Egypt and exceeded all bounds by claiming lordship. The scholars agree on the intensity of the fear and on Pharaoh as its source, but differ over the meaning of "dhurriyya" and the referent of the pronoun in "qawmihi". Ibn 'Abbas in one report, Qatada and al-Dahhak take it to mean a few people, while Mujahid, whom al-Tabari follows, understands the children of those to whom Moses was sent, whose fathers had died over a long time. Ibn 'Abbas in another report, with Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, identifies them as the Children of Israel; others, including 'Atiyya, identify them as members of Pharaoh's household, such as his wife, the believer from Pharaoh's family, or his treasurer. Al-Farra' explains that they are called descendants because their fathers were Copts and their mothers Israelites. The pronoun "mala'ihim" is taken by some to refer to Pharaoh and his court, and by others to the descendants, the view al-Tabari prefers. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir lean toward the pronoun in "qawmihi" referring to Pharaoh, since the Children of Israel all believed in Moses, while al-Razi and Abu Hayyan favour Moses as the closer antecedent. Most read "an yaftinahum" as torture, killing, or turning them away from their religion.

The commentators explain that Moses, seeing his people afraid of Pharaoh, told them that if they truly believed in God they should rely on Him alone, provided they were submitting to Him. They replied that they relied on God and asked Him not to make them a trial for the wrongdoing people. Most exegetes agree that tawakkul means trust in God, leaving one's affairs to Him, and that submission here means sincere surrender and single-hearted devotion, so the second condition completes the first, since genuine reliance cannot coexist with a divided heart. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir read the plea as asking that God not give the oppressors power over them, lest they think themselves rightful and grow more obstinate. Mujahid understands it as a request not to be punished by Pharaoh's people or by a direct divine punishment, lest the enemies say that the believers would not be punished if they were righteous; Abu Mijlaz and Abu al-Duha give the first reading. Al-Zamakhshari combines both readings. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that some take fitna as torment or killing. Al-Razi notes that the order of the request, placing the protection of the religion before the protection of the self, shows concern for faith. Many commentators connect the verse with what follows, where Moses and Aaron instruct the Israelites to make their homes places of prayer, since Pharaoh had forbidden their houses of worship.

This verse reports the reply of Moses' believing people when their prophet told them to rely on God if they were believers and submitters. They answered that they relied on God alone, then asked not to be made a trial for the wrongdoing people. The commentators broadly agree on the meaning. Mujahid, Ibn Abi Najih and al-Tabari, followed by Ibn Kathir, explain that they asked that Pharaoh and his people not be allowed to torment them, lest those people say that if they were upon truth they would not be punished, and so be led astray. Abu Mijlaz and Abu al-Duha, in one report cited by Ibn Kathir, understood it as a request that the unbelievers not prevail over them, lest they think themselves better and persist in their rebellion. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi allow that the trial may be a place of punishment or a cause of misguidance. Al-Razi reads the word as meaning those who are tried, that is, a request that the oppressors not be enabled to force them away from their religion. Ibn al-Qayyim also records views that God not restrict their provision. Several scholars, among them al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud, note that the believers put the safety of their faith before the safety of their own lives. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the repeated condition stresses the sincerity of faith and that trust in God is bound to faith and submission. Ibn 'Atiyya adds that reliance on God is joined with taking lawful means.

In this verse Moses and his people ask their Lord to deliver them by His mercy from the disbelieving people, meaning Pharaoh and his court, who had enslaved them and forced them into hard and degrading labour, as al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi explain. Commentators link this request to Moses' call on his people to rely on God, and to their answer, 'In God we have put our trust', followed by their prayer, 'Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people'. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Biqa'i observe that placing trust before the supplication shows that one who prays should base his prayer on reliance upon God. Al-Razi notes that they ask first for the protection of their faith and only then for their own deliverance, which shows that their concern for religion outweighed their concern for their own safety. Abu Hayyan and al-Baydawi add that the word 'mercy' expresses humility, since deliverance comes from God and not from the merit of the believers. On the meaning of 'deliver', al-Sha'rawi compares it to a high place safe from the flood, while Ibn 'Ashur sees it as protection from the harm and violence of the unbelievers. Al-Jaza'iri and the Muyassar simply take it as rescue from their oppression. The commentaries do not draw any legal ruling from this verse, which concerns the trust and prayer of believers facing injustice.

This verse records the command God revealed to Moses and his brother Aaron: to settle homes for their people in Egypt, to make those houses places of prayer facing the qibla, to establish the prayer, and to give good news to the believers. According to Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima, al-Nakha'i and al-Dahhak, cited by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, Pharaoh had forbidden the Children of Israel to pray in their churches and places of worship and had destroyed them, so they were ordered to make mosques within their homes and pray there out of fear of him. Ibn Kathir sees in this an instruction to pray more often in the face of hardship.

Most commentators agree that the word "houses" here means mosques and that the qibla is the direction of prayer. They differ on what it was. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Farra' and al-Nasafi identify it as the Ka'ba, which Ibn Abbas describes as the qibla of Moses and his people, while al-Baghawi also reports the view that it was Jerusalem. Sa'id ibn Jubayr understands rather that the houses should face one another. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi prefer the first reading.

Opinions also differ on Misr: Mujahid takes it to be Alexandria, while al-Dahhak takes it as the well-known land of Egypt. Several scholars, including al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Qayyim, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan, note that the verse addresses Moses and Aaron first, then the whole people for prayer, and finally Moses alone for the good news, since he is the foundation of the mission. Ibn Ashur, for his part, suggests these dwellings were tents prepared for departure.

This passage records Moses' prayer against Pharaoh and his chiefs, after God had given them adornment and wealth in this world, which the commentators understand became a cause of their going astray. Most exegetes agree on the request: O Lord, obliterate or transform their wealth, harden their hearts so that they do not soften to faith, and let them not believe until they see the painful punishment, which Ibn 'Abbas explained as drowning. On the lam in "liyudillu", opinions differ: al-Khalil and Sibawayh take it as the lam of consequence, meaning that their end was misguidance, as in "that they might have an enemy and a grief"; al-Farra' and al-Tabari take it as a lam of purpose or testing, in the sense of a means of trial; az-Zamakhshari takes it as a lam of supplication. Some read it as "lest they go astray", with a negation understood. On the meaning of tamsa, Mujahid and 'Atiyya say destruction and effacement, while most say a change of form, and Qatada, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd report that their money, dinars, dirhams and crops turned to stone. On "so they will not believe", al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i take it as a jussive of supplication, while al-Akhfash takes it as a subjunctive answering the imperative. On "your prayer has been answered", Ibn 'Abbas and others report that Moses prayed while Aaron said amen, so the one who says amen shares in the supplication; others note that the answer came only after forty years. Some commentators add that a prophet may curse his people only with divine permission.

The commentators explain that this verse records God's response to Moses' supplication against Pharaoh and his chiefs, who persisted in disbelief despite their wealth and splendour. God tells Moses and Aaron that their prayer has been answered, and commands them to remain steadfast in their mission and not to follow the way of those who do not know, that is, not to hasten what God has promised. Most of them agree that Moses was the one supplicating while Aaron said amen, which is why the answer is attributed to both; Ibn 'Atiyya and others note that amen is itself a form of supplication, and that the dual can refer to one person, as Arab poets show. On the delay, al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir relay from Ibn Jurayj and Muhammad ibn 'Ali that Pharaoh remained forty years after the prayer, while Ibn Kathir also cites Muhammad ibn 'Ali for forty days. As to the meaning of istaqima, al-Suddi and al-Tabari take it as pressing on with God's command and leaving with the people, al-Baghawi and others as persevering in the call, and al-Nasafi as patience without haste. Regarding the prohibition against following those who do not know, most see it as a warning against impatience with God's promise, while some identify those people as Pharaoh and his folk. Al-Razi draws a theological argument from the lam of liyudillu, which others read as the lam of consequence, and the readers differ on the vowelling of the verb.

The verse describes how God brought the Children of Israel across the sea, while Pharaoh and his armies pursued them in injustice and aggression. When drowning overtook him, he declared that he believed there is no god but the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and that he was among those who submit. The commentators agree that the pursuit was a seeking of dominance without right in speech and injustice in action, and that this profession came at the moment of punishment and was not accepted, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi explain. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate that Gabriel then pushed mud into Pharaoh's mouth out of fear that mercy would reach him. Al-Zamakhshari considers this an addition by slanderers, whereas Ibn Hajar replies that the hadith is sound and admits a sound explanation, and al-Razi counts it among the reasons the faith was rejected. Some commentators hold that the body was saved as a lifeless form, while al-Qurtubi notes that it was cast onto the shore so the Israelites could see it. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi see the episode as visible proof of Pharaoh's death, and al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi take it as a sign and lesson for those who come after him. Al-Jaza'iri and al-Sa'di stress that faith professed at the moment of death is not accepted, since repentance remains valid only before the vision of punishment.

The commentators explain that this verse recounts God's response to Pharaoh when drowning overtook him and he said: I believe there is no god but the One in whom the Children of Israel believed, and I am among the submitters. The reply is a rebuke: do you believe now, when you disobeyed before and were among the corrupters? They agree that faith at the moment of distress does not benefit him, and that repentance in the face of punishment is not accepted. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan hold that faith at the onset of punishment is not accepted, citing the verse: their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might. They differ on who spoke these words: al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi name God, Gabriel or Michael, while others take them as Pharaoh's own thoughts. As for the phrase today We shall save you in your body, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the sea cast up his lifeless body on a height so that the Children of Israel, who doubted his death, could see it; others understand his armour, and Mujahid his body. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi cite the hadith in which Gabriel pushed mud into Pharaoh's mouth lest mercy reach him; al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim graded it sound, al-Zamakhshari rejected it, and Ibn Hajar replied. All close with the statement that many people are heedless of Our signs.

God says that He will bring Pharaoh out of the depths of the sea after his drowning and cast his body, intact, onto a raised place, so that it would be a sign for those who come after him, who would see that he was a weak servant and not the lord he claimed to be. The commentators broadly agree on this meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it that the body was displayed to the Children of Israel, who doubted his death, and al-Tabari supports this with reports from Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Abbas. They differ on the sense of "with your body": Mujahid and most exegetes say it means the body without a soul, while Abu Sakhr, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and others say it means his armour, which was known to be adorned with gold or pearls; al-Akhfash considered that view unfounded. The reading with the letter ha, "nunahhika", attributed to Ibn Mas'ud and Yazid, means he was thrown on the shore. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the passage also concerns Pharaoh's faith at the moment of death, which al-Razi explains with several reasons. As to the sign, most hold that it is addressed to the Children of Israel or to later generations; Ibn Kathir relates a hadith in which Gabriel stuffed mud into Pharaoh's mouth. The verse ends by noting that many people are heedless of God's signs, meaning they do not reflect or take warning from them; Muqatil took this to refer to the people of Mecca, while al-Hasan gave it a general sense.

God tells us that He settled the Children of Israel in an honourable and pleasing dwelling and provided them with good things. The commentators differ on the place: al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Zayd take it to be Syria and Jerusalem, al-Dahhak Egypt and Syria, while Ibn Abbas names Jordan and Palestine. As for the words 'they did not differ until knowledge came to them', most commentators read them as referring to the shared expectation of the prophet foretold in their scriptures: they split when the Quran or Muhammad came, some believing and others rejecting him. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi also understand a split after reading the Torah. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi take 'knowledge' to mean 'what is known', that is Muhammad, a view Ibn al-Jawzi also reports, citing Ibn Abbas. Al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that this disagreement cannot be resolved in this world and that God will judge between the parties on the Day of Resurrection, separating truth from falsehood. The commentators do not decide between these views but present them side by side, and all agree that the verse censures disagreement after the truth has become clear.

The verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ in conditional form: if he has any doubt about what has been revealed to him, he should ask those who read the Scripture before him, for the truth has come to him from his Lord, so he must not be among the doubters. The commentators agree that doubt cannot truly be attributed to the Prophet, and that the address, though apparently to him, is meant for others, as in the verse "O Prophet, when you divorce women." Ibn Kathir reports, with Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and Qatada, that the Prophet said: "I do not doubt and I do not ask." As to whom one should ask, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak identify them as the People of the Book who believed, such as Abdullah ibn Salam, whom Ibn Zayd names explicitly. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read the condition as a supposition, and al-Farra' compares it to the Arab way of telling one's son, "if you are my son, be dutiful to me," with no doubt involved. Al-Zajjaj takes the particle in as negative, meaning "ma." Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi hold that the address is to all listeners or to the believers. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi also note that doubt may mean a constriction of the heart, the Prophet's patience with his people's refusal. Most exegetes see the verse as establishing the proof against the opponents through the testimony of the People of the Book, and as continuing with the statement that those upon whom the Lord's word has been fulfilled will not believe even if every sign comes to them.

This verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ, yet most commentators hold that the intended audience is others, namely the believers and listeners, in a familiar Arabic mode of address. He is forbidden to be among those who denied God's signs, lest he forfeit God's mercy and pleasure and fall into wrath and punishment. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, followed by al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Sa'di, take the address as meant for others. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi read it as a rhetorical stirring and reinforcement directed at the Prophet, and as a strong warning about how ugly denial is. Regarding the preceding verse, 'if you are in doubt', opinions differ: al-Farra' and al-Hasan read the particle in as a negation, while most take it as conditional, the doubt being hypothetical. Al-Tabari reports from Ibn Abbas that the Prophet never doubted nor asked. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur note that the people of the Book consulted are mainly those who embraced Islam, such as Abdullah ibn Salam, though the point is debated. Al-Zamakhshari stresses that mentioning the People of the Book praises their learning rather than accusing the Prophet of doubt. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the verse alludes to the polytheists, and that the prohibitions on doubt and denial warn of the loss that befalls those who commit them.

This verse states that those upon whom the word of your Lord has been fulfilled will not believe, even if every sign comes to them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others explain that this word is God's wrath and curse upon those who disobey Him, so their faith is of no use at the time when it would have benefited them, namely before they see the painful punishment, as happened to Pharaoh. Al-Zamakhshari takes the word to be a known decree written in the Preserved Tablet, that these people will die as disbelievers, while al-Razi and Abu Hayyan speak of God's eternal will and decree. Al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud agree that it is a divine decree that cannot be reversed. Ibn 'Atiyya says God fixed their wrath from eternity and created them for punishment, and that the verse warns people to hasten to faith before punishment comes. Ibn Kathir adds that the People of the Book recognise the Prophet as they recognise their own sons, yet they distort and conceal this. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read 'kalimat' in the plural, while the others read 'kalima' in the singular. Many commentators mention the people of Jonah, who were spared because they believed before the punishment fell. Al-Tabari held that they repented after seeing the punishment, but Ibn 'Atiyya rejected this, defining the sight that prevents repentance as the punishment or death actually reaching a person. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as discouraging hope in the faith of stubborn people who are not moved by proof.

This passage states that those upon whom the word of your Lord has been fulfilled will not believe, even if every sign came to them. Al-Tabari explains the word as God's wrath and punishment for their disobedience, a view echoed by Mujahid and Qatada. Al-Baghawi reports that it may mean the curse, or God's saying that these are in the Fire and He does not care. Al-Razi, Ibn Juzayy and most exegetes read the verse as the certainty of a decree that cannot be overturned, while al-Zamakhshari takes the word as a written knowledge in the Preserved Tablet, a reading that Sunni commentators such as Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi reject because they hold that God wills all that occurs. Ibn 'Atiyya sees a warning meant to urge people to faith before it is too late. For most commentators, faith does not benefit once the painful punishment is seen, as with Pharaoh. They point to the people of Yunus, who believed in time and were spared, though al-Tabari treats them as a special case while Ibn 'Atiyya disagrees. Some hold that they saw the punishment itself and others only its signs, following al-Zajjaj. On recitation, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read the word as plural, the others as singular. The feminine verb is explained by the grammarians as agreement with the following word āya.

This verse states that no town which rejected its messengers was saved by its faith when it saw the punishment, except the people of Yunus, who believed before the torment fell on them; God lifted from them the punishment of disgrace in this worldly life and let them enjoy life until their appointed term. Most commentators place this story at Nineveh, in the region of Mosul. When they lost their prophet and feared the approaching punishment, they put on coarse garments, separated mothers from their young, and cried out to God, who had mercy on them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that their faith was accepted after they saw the punishment close at hand, or even with their own eyes, while al-Zajjaj, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur say they saw only the signs of the punishment, and that their repentance came before that. As for the exception, most grammarians and exegetes treat it as disconnected, meaning 'but the people of Yunus', while some take it as connected in the sense of negation; a nominative reading as an apposition is also reported. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the verse an indirect address to the Meccans, urged to believe before punishment arrives. Ibn Sa'di notes that faith forced by fear is not true faith, and that the exception rests on a wisdom known to God. The narrative also includes traditions about the invocation 'Ya Hayy, hina la hayy' and the restitution of stolen property, and it is said to have occurred on the day of Ashura; the commentators do not settle between these views.

This verse states that had your Lord willed, everyone on earth would have believed together, without exception, but He did not will it, and the Prophet ﷺ cannot force people to believe. The Prophet was very eager that all people should believe, and the verse comforts and eases him. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that only the one for whom happiness was decreed in the first Book believes, and only the one for whom wretchedness was decreed goes astray, and Ibn Kathir adds that God guides whom He wills and leads astray whom He wills, by His knowledge, wisdom and justice. The commentators agree that compulsion to faith is impossible, since faith is an act of the heart that cannot be produced by force.

The meaning of God's "willing" has however divided them. Al-Zamakhshari, as reported by Abu Hayyan, and al-Baydawi report that the Mu'tazilites read it as a will of compulsion, which the Sunni scholars reject. Al-Razi judges this reading weak, since forced faith would be of no benefit, while al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi see the verse as a rebuttal of the Qadariyya. The phrase "by God's permission" is understood by Ibn 'Ashur as the capacity of understanding, and by al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi as God's decree.

Whether the verse was abrogated was also debated. Muqatil, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi report that it was abrogated by the verse of the sword, while Ibn al-Jawzi himself and Ibn Juzayy regard it as unabrogated. As for "rijs", Ibn 'Abbas takes it to mean wrath, al-Hasan and al-Farra' punishment, Mujahid what holds no good, and Qatada the devil, according to the reports cited by Abu Hayyan and al-Suyuti.

This verse states that no soul can believe except by Allah's permission, meaning His will, His enabling grace and His decree, and that the Prophet is not charged with forcing people to faith. The commentators explain this permission in closely related ways: al-Thawri and Ibn Abbas take it as God's decree and command, Ata as His will, and others as His knowledge or the facilitation of His favour, al-Zamakhshari speaking of the granting of gracious help. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di recall that God guides whom He wills and misguides whom He wills, in keeping with His wisdom. The word rijs has been given several meanings: divine wrath according to Ibn Abbas, punishment according to al-Farra', al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj, what is impure according to Mujahid, sin according to Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Satan according to Qatada, and forsaking by God, which causes punishment, according to al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi. All agree that those who do not understand are those who do not use their reason to reflect on God's signs and proofs. Abu Hayyan reports the Mu'tazili debate on compulsion and will, while al-Razi refutes their position and holds that faith comes from God's creation and will. Some read the verb with nun, others read rijz with zay. As for the preceding verse, al-Mawardi and others see it as a consolation to the Prophet, while Ibn Juzayy and others report that it concerns the early period of Islam before being abrogated by the verse of the sword.

God instructs His Prophet to tell the polytheists to reflect and consider what lies in the heavens and on earth, signs that point to God's oneness: the sun, the moon, the alternation of night and day, rain, mountains, seas and plants. The commentators see this reflection as the way to know God. As for the next phrase, "Yet signs and warnings avail nothing for a people who do not believe," al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi explain that signs and messengers do not benefit those whom God has known, in His foreknowledge, will not believe, since they refuse to learn from the proofs out of stubbornness. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Nasafi take "ma" as a negation, while others allow it to be interrogative, meaning a rebuke. Ibn 'Atiyya also reports a reading in which the verse urges faith, using the people of Yunus as an example. On abrogation, al-Tabari and others consider the verse clear, while Ibn 'Atiyya reports that some hold it abrogated by the verse of the sword, without deciding between the views. The Jalalayn and al-Baghawi identify the warners with the messengers. Al-Sa'di explains that those who do not benefit from the signs are those who turn away and persist in obstinacy.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ that the idolaters of his people await nothing after their denial but what befell the nations before them, namely God's dealings with them, as He struck Noah's people, 'Ad and Thamud. The Arabs used the word "days" for such events. He then tells him to say: wait, then, and I am waiting with you. The commentators agree that the verse is a threat and a warning, while deliverance belongs to the messengers and to those who believed. Qatada and al-Rabi' ibn Anas explain that the "days" are God's punishments of earlier peoples, and that God first warned them and then announced the rescue of His messengers and the believers. al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir, al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti, and al-Sa'di share this reading. They differ on what the rescue is: al-Rabi' takes it as deliverance from punishment in this world, while Muqatil takes it as protection from the Fire in the next. On the phrase "a binding promise upon Us", al-Zamakhshari treats it as a parenthesis meaning that this is absolutely due, al-Razi argues it is due by promise and decree rather than by any merit of the servant, and al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan offer related readings. Ibn 'Atiyya sees the "wait" as a temporary truce later abrogated by the command to fight. Hafs and al-Kisa'i read the verb with a lighter form, others with a doubled one, with the same meaning.

This verse states that when punishment strikes the deniers, God saves His messengers and those who believed with them, and that this is His established practice toward earlier nations. Al-Tabari paraphrases it as: await the days of past peoples who perished by God's punishment; then Muhammad and those who believed in him will be saved, as God did for the earlier messengers, and this deliverance is a binding truth on Him. Al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Baydawi agree that the verse is at once a warning to unbelievers and good news for believers, with deliverance tied to faith. Qatada identifies the 'days' of those who passed with God's dealings with the peoples of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, the Arabs also calling punishment and blessings 'days'. Az-Zamakhshari reads 'then' as linking to an implied statement: We destroy the nations, then We save Our messengers. On the word 'thus', opinions differ: az-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi take it as referring to a similar rescue, while several treat 'a truth upon Us' as a parenthetical clause. Ar-Razi reports the judge's view that this rescue is obligatory because of God's promise and decree rather than any merit owed by the servant. The reading of al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Ya'qub with the lighter form is equivalent in meaning to the intensive form used by the others. Ibn al-Jawzi gives two interpretations of the deliverance: being spared the punishment in this world when it descends, or being spared the Fire in the hereafter.

God commands His Prophet to address the people, meaning the polytheists of Mecca and others, and to tell them that if they doubt his religion, he himself does not doubt it, and that he does not worship the idols they worship besides God. He worships God who causes people to die and takes their souls at their appointed times, and he has been commanded to be among the believers. The commentators, including al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, generally explain that the doubt that truly makes sense is doubt about worshipping idols that neither harm nor benefit, not doubt about the Prophet's religion. Al-Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baydawi see the mention of God causing death as a warning, because death is the appointed time of punishment for the polytheists. Ibn 'Ashur and Abu Hayyan note that the doubt may concern the truth of the religion or the Prophet's steadfastness in it. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi hold that the command to worship is known by reason and by revelation together. Al-Razi observes that the rejection of worshipping others comes before the affirmation of worshipping God. As for the command to set one's face toward the religion as a hanif, al-Mawardi lists several meanings: a pilgrim, a sincere worshipper, a follower, one who is upright, or one who believes in all the prophets. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi connect it to the prohibition of associating partners with God. Several scholars, such as Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi, consider parts of this passage abrogated by the command to fight, while al-Sha'rawi sees this separation as a lasting break with the polytheists.

God commands His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, as the commentators explain, to set his face and his whole self upon the upright religion, to remain steadfast in it and to be devoted to it wholly, and never to be among those who associate partners with God. Ibn 'Abbas interprets "your face" as "your deed", while others take it to mean "your self", so the sense is sincerity of action and firmness in what one has been commanded. Most exegetes read "and that I should stand firm" as coordinated with "that I should be among the believers". Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur offer other grammatical analyses of the particle "an" and of an implied verb, which they treat as points of syntax rather than the core meaning. On the word "hanif" the scholars differ: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, 'Ata' and al-Suddi take it to mean a pilgrim, Mujahid a follower, Muhammad ibn Ka'b upright, 'Ata' sincere, Abu Qilaba one who believes in all the messengers, and al-Razi a total inclination away from everything other than God. There is broad agreement that the hanifiyya is the religion of Abraham, free from associationism. Al-Razi and al-Baghawi note that this command follows the statement that worship is due to God alone, so faith is the foundation and sincerity its fruit, and although addressed to the Prophet it concerns the whole community. Ibn Juzayy reports that some scholars regard the following part of the command as abrogated by the verses on fighting.

In this verse God commands His Prophet ﷺ not to call upon, or worship, anything besides God that can neither benefit him if he does so nor harm him if he refrains, and He declares that whoever does so is among the wrongdoers. The commentators generally understand the prohibition as a ban on worshipping idols, with al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir taking the verb to mean worship, while as-Samʿani gives it the senses of both calling out and asking. They agree that the wrongdoing here is polytheism, since it places worship where it does not belong, as az-Zamakhshari, an-Nasafi and Ibn ʿAshur state, though al-Tabari reads it as wronging oneself. Al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir observe that the Prophet is addressed while the warning is meant for others, and Abu as-Suʿud and Ibn ʿAshur explain that the conditional form shows there is no excuse for one who does what has been forbidden. Al-Razi draws a mystical reading, holding that nothing acts except God. On abrogation, Ibn ʿAbbas, reported by al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, says the verse was abrogated by the verse on fighting, but the other commentators do not mention this for this verse. Shinqiti and Sha'rawi stress that idols possess no power to help or harm, which makes calling on them meaningless.

This verse states that harm and good both lie in God's hands alone: if God afflicts the Prophet with hardship, none can remove it but Him, and if He wills good for him, none can turn back His bounty. The commentators, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi, agree that it denies the idols any power to harm or benefit and affirms God's exclusive power over both. Although addressed to the Prophet, its meaning is understood as a rebuke to the polytheists and a warning to believers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the bounty to mean ease and health, whereas al-Razi and Abu Hayyan extend it to every good God decrees. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud note that good is linked to the verb of will and harm to the verb of touching, so that al-Razi concludes good is intended for its own sake and harm only incidentally. Ibn al-Qayyim draws from it the duty to trust God alone and to be grateful for His favours. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Tabarsi and al-Jaza'iri report that some scholars judged part of the surrounding context abrogated by the verse on fighting, while others, such as Ibn Ashur, reject abrogation here. The closing words, 'the Forgiving, the Merciful', are read by al-Tabari as pardon for whoever repents, even from polytheism according to Ibn Kathir. Ibn Ashur adds that the divine will is deliberately left unspecified so that people pursue every path toward the bounty.

This verse addresses the Prophet, telling him to say to people that the truth has come to them from their Lord, so that no one has any excuse left. Whoever is guided benefits only himself, and whoever goes astray bears the harm only on himself. The Prophet then states that he is not a guardian over them and cannot compel them to be guided; he is only a messenger who conveys the message and a warner, as al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di explain.

Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur, understand the Truth to mean the Quran or Islam. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi add that it may refer to the Prophet himself, and al-Qurtubi also gives this as one view. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir stress that the benefit of guidance returns to the one who is guided and the burden of error falls on the one who strays. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan present a reading linked to predestination: whoever is decreed in eternity to be guided will be, and whoever is decreed to stray will stray, which is the Sunni position. Al-Razi also cites the Mu'tazili judge al-Qadi, who holds that the verse shows the Sharia is complete and no excuse remains. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the particles lam and 'ala convey benefit and harm.

The commentators disagree on abrogation. Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya, held that the verse was abrogated by the verse of fighting. Others, including Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan, consider it unabrogated and read "I am not a guardian over you" as meaning he does not hold them accountable for their deeds. For the following verse on patience, al-Zamakhshari relates the hadith about the Ansar enduring the favouritism of rulers.

This verse commands the Prophet ﷺ to follow what is revealed to him, to act upon it and convey it, and to be patient with the opposition and harm of the polytheists until God judges between them, granting him victory, for He is the best of judges. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi explain this judgment as victory and dominance over his enemies. Al-Jaza'iri links it to the battle of Badr and the fighting against the polytheists, while al-Shinqiti points to several verses announcing victory and the spread of the religion. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi read the patience as steadfastness in the truth, and al-Tha'alibi cites the hadith about the easy and tolerant faith. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan report that after this verse the Prophet ﷺ gathered the Ansar and told them to be patient with the favouritism of rulers, and they recount the story of Mu'awiya and Abu Qatada. Al-Sam'ani, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur focus on the nature of patience as enduring hardship and persisting in obedience. On abrogation, Ibn Abbas, al-Wahidi, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Tabari say the verse was abrogated by the verse of fighting. Abu Hayyan notes that others consider it unabrogated, understanding patience as obedience and bearing the mission, and that the most careful scholars take this view. The commentators do not settle these views and present them side by side.
